phonemes.desc: Short open-mid front [ɛ], as in English 'elf'; the light, unstressed first syllable.
Voiced labiodental [v]: Welsh writes the v-sound with a single f — the name's first trap for English eyes.
Alveolar nasal [n], short [ɪ] (the Welsh y of a non-final syllable), and [s]; this is the stressed syllable — Welsh words carry their weight on the penult.
Palatal glide [j] and short open [ɛ] closing on [n]; the final syllable falls away unstressed, 'yen' kept light.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ev-NIS-yen' — the f sounds as v, the stress lands on the middle syllable, and the last syllable is a quick, light 'yen'.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Efnisien, son of Euroswydd and Penarddun, in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest

kin.label: The named opposite
kin.form: Nisien, his brother — the tale presents the two as one contrast: peace-maker and strife-maker

kin.label: English translations
kin.form: Efnisien (Guest), Efnysien — the same name carried into English prose

pronunciation.note: Efnysien is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh manuscript form is written in plain Latin letters, and normalized Welsh orthography attaches no diacritic to the name — there is nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the figure's weight in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Trouble, Mischief
domains.subtitle: The Strife-Maker of the Second Branch, and the Cauldron He Died Breaking
domains.lead: Efnysien is the destroyer of the Mabinogi: the man the Second Branch introduces in a single balanced sentence — his brother Nisien could make peace between two armies at their most embittered; Efnysien could make two brothers quarrel when they loved each other best. One act of his, the maiming of the Irish king's horses, sets two kingdoms on the road to ruin; his last act, the breaking of the Cauldron of Rebirth, costs him his heart and ends the slaughter he began.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: At the wedding feast of Aberffraw, in a rage that no one had asked his consent, he cuts the lips, ears, tails, and eyelids of Matholwch's horses — the insult that compensation could not bury.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Pair Dadeni — the vessel Brân gives in compensation: a slain man thrown in today rises tomorrow a fighting man, but speechless. Efnysien dies stretching it to pieces.

cards.name: The Hundred Bags
cards.desc: In the great house the Irish built for Brân, a hundred armed men hide in flour-bags hung on the pillars. Efnysien walks the row, asks what is in each bag, and crushes a skull through the sacking with his fingers.

cards.name: The Boy in the Fire
cards.desc: At the peace feast his nephew Gwern — Branwen's child, newly made king — goes from lap to lap; at Efnysien's lap he is seized and thrown into the flames. After that there is no peace to be made.

symbols.name: The mutilated horses
symbols.meaning: Pride made visible — an insult so literal that no payment could make the injured king forget it

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth (Pair Dadeni)
symbols.meaning: War stripped of death's limit — the gift that became a weapon, until the one who broke it broke himself

symbols.name: The flour-bags on the pillars
symbols.meaning: Treachery hidden in hospitality — seen through only by the man whose own mind worked that way

symbols.name: Gwern cast into the flames
symbols.meaning: The murder of the heir at the moment of his investiture — the point past which the tale permits no return

symbols.name: The broken heart
symbols.meaning: His only death-wound: he stretched himself inside the cauldron until it burst into four pieces, and his heart broke with it

mythology.lead: Efnysien belongs to one tale and fills it: the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr. The branch is the story of a compensation that failed, and Efnysien is the reason — twice over the author of the injury, and at the end the author of the only sacrifice that stopped the ruin.

myths.title: The Two Brothers
myths.text: The tale introduces him by contrast. Penarddun ferch Beli, mother of Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan by Llŷr, bore two sons to Euroswydd: Nisien and Efnysien. Of Nisien the branch says he was a good man and a gentle youth, who could bring peace between two armies at their most embittered; of Efnysien it says he would set two brothers at strife when they loved each other most. The whole Second Branch is the working-out of that one sentence.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text: When Brân gave his half-sister Branwen to Matholwch, king of Ireland, the wedding feast was held at Aberffraw, and the horses of the Irish king were stabled for the night. Efnysien asked why they were there, and was told they belonged to Matholwch, who had married his sister. 'Is this what they have done with a maiden as fine as her, my own sister — given her away without asking me?' In his rage he went under the horses and cut off their lips to the teeth, their ears to the head, their tails to the rumps, and their eyelids to the bone. Matholwch rose in silence and made for his ships; only Brân's embassy — Manawydan among them — and the offer of honour-price brought him back: a silver staff as tall as himself, a gold plate as broad as his face, fresh horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth, which Brân had from Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, wanderers who had fled to his court out of Ireland.

myths.title: The Hundred Bags of Flour
myths.text: The compensation did not hold. In Ireland the insult was remembered, Matholwch was shamed by his own nobles, and Branwen was sent to the kitchen with a box on the ear from the butcher every day — until she tamed a starling and sent word across the sea. Brân waded the channel, for no ship could carry him, and lay across the river when the Irish destroyed the bridge: 'He who would be a leader, let him be a bridge.' The Irish sued for terms: the kingship would pass to Gwern, Branwen's son, and they would build Brân a house great enough to hold him — the first house he had ever entered. But in that house they hung a hundred bags, an armed man in each. Efnysien walked the row ahead of the feast, laid his hand on each bag — 'What is in here?' 'Flour.' — and squeezed each head through the sacking until he felt the skull give, a hundred times down the hall.

myths.title: The Boy in the Fire
myths.text: At the feast of reconciliation the boy Gwern was invested as king, and — charming everyone, the branch says — he went from lap to lap among his kinsmen, from Brân to Manawydan to Nisien, until he came to Efnysien's lap. 'Why does my nephew not come to me?' Efnysien asked; and when the boy was put into his arms he seized him by the feet and threw him headlong into the great fire. Branwen would have leapt in after her son, but Brân caught her with one hand and took up his shield with the other, and the hall rose in war. It is the tale's darkest sentence, and its hinge: after Gwern, no negotiation is possible.

myths.title: The Breaking of the Cauldron
myths.text: In the battle that followed, the Irish had the advantage that could not be beaten: every night they cast their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth, and every morning the dead rose as fighting men again — speechless, but unkillable in any final sense. Then Efnysien, seeing the ruin he had made, did the one thing only he could do. He lay down among the Irish dead as if he were a corpse, was thrown into the cauldron with them, and stretched himself out inside it until the vessel burst into four pieces — and his own heart burst with it, and so he died. The branch gives him no speech of repentance and no eulogy: the destroyer ends the war his own hand started, at the price of his life, and the narration passes on. Of the hosts of Britain only seven men came home, bearing Brân's head; Branwen died of a broken heart on the shore of Anglesey and was buried in a four-sided grave on the bank of the Alaw.

lore.syncretism: The comparison that follows Efnysien everywhere is with [[loki|Loki]]: the malice inside the house, the sworn kin whose mischief costs the gods their peace, the trickster the tale can neither spare nor save. MacKillop and the handbooks register the parallel as typological rather than genealogical — the Mabinogi's strife-maker is a human prince of the Children of Llŷr, not a god, and his story answers to Welsh concerns: the honour-price, the insult remembered, the compensation that fails. The truer Celtic company is the cauldron-complex: the Cauldron of Rebirth belongs to the same deep stock as the Dagda's cauldron from Murias in the Lebor Gabála Érenn, from which no company went away unsatisfied, and the branch itself gives the vessel an Irish provenance through the fugitive Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. Within the corpus his closest kin are [[nisien|Nisien]], the brother he was written as the opposite of, and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the king his pride destroyed; [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and [[taliesin|Taliesin]] are among the seven who carried Brân's head home.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the Second Branch into the English-speaking world, and Efnysien's maiming of the horses and death in the cauldron became set-pieces of the Victorian Celtic revival. Evangeline Walton retold the branch at full length in The Children of Llyr (1971), the second volume of her Mabinogion tetralogy, and gave him the modern novel's inside view without softening him. His widest-reaching legacy is the cauldron itself: Lloyd Alexander drew the deathless cauldron-born warriors of his Prydain chronicles — The Black Cauldron (1965), filmed by Disney in 1985 — directly from the Welsh matter, where a cauldron that returns the slain to silent service is broken at terrible cost. In Welsh memory the branch left two landmarks: the proverb 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and Bedd Branwen, the grave by the Alaw where the tradition buried the sister his acts helped kill.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Efnysien is what a story looks like when it refuses to flatter anyone — including itself. The Second Branch never explains him. He is not possessed, not wronged first, not mad; the tale simply pairs him with Nisien and lets the contrast stand: what one brother binds, the other unbinds, and the world has both kinds of man in it. His evil is small in scale and total in consequence — a night with a knife in a stable, and two kingdoms bleed for a generation. That is the branch's hardest teaching about trouble: it does not need to be great, only timely, and no compensation is large enough to make an injured king forget.

And then the ending, which the Welsh text declines to call redemption. Efnysien sees what his mischief has cost — the speechless dead rising nightly from the cauldron — and lies down among the corpses of the enemy to be thrown in with them. No one forgives him in the text; no one praises him; the branch records only that the cauldron broke and his heart broke. The destroyer is allowed one act of destruction aimed at destruction itself, and it costs exactly everything he has. The Mabinogi does not promise that the man who sets the fire can put it out. It shows him choosing to burn with it.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Efnisien — Middle Welsh (Brythonic Celtic), attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), recording material composed centuries earlier. The normalized form writes plain Latin letters with no diacritic, so the restoration Efnysien differs from the ASCII input only in the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: efnysien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Efnysien is an entirely literary figure: no inscription, cult site, or votive deposit names him, and the Welsh theonymic record of the period survives in literature rather than stone. His evidence is manuscript evidence — the Second Branch complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with the tales' composition argued to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Aberffraw, the royal court of Gwynedd where the horses were maimed; Harlech, where Brân's court sat; and the shore of Anglesey where the survivors landed. The tradition's one material anchor is Bedd Branwen, a cairn on the bank of the Afon Alaw in Anglesey identified since the Middle Ages with Branwen's 'four-sided grave' — excavated by Frances Lynch in 1967–68 and found to hold Early Bronze Age cremations, far older than any Mabinogi event: the identification is the folklore, not the archaeology, and it is precisely that honesty the record keeps.
